Short_Definition: Time from randomisation to first PRO score worsening meeting a predefined threshold.
Extended_Definition: TTD is a time-to-event endpoint measuring the interval from randomisation to the first observed decline in a patient-reported outcome score that meets or exceeds a predefined clinically meaningful threshold, typically the MID. It is analysed using Kaplan-Meier estimation and Cox proportional hazards regression, with patients who do not deteriorate, withdraw, or die censored at last assessment. TTD is sensitive to threshold choice, assessment schedule, and censoring rules — all of which must be pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan. FDA and EMA increasingly require TTD alongside survival endpoints to capture the patient's symptomatic experience of treatment. In multiple myeloma trials, TTD is commonly applied to pain, fatigue, and global health status using EORTC QLQ-C30 or FACT-MM.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: TTD directly operationalises continuous PRO data as a formal, testable endpoint, enabling regulatory labelling claims about symptom preservation or delay of worsening. Its statistical and methodological choices (threshold, censoring, instrument) require explicit justification in submissions.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Time to PRO deterioration | Time to symptom deterioration | Time to health status deterioration | Time to first deterioration | Time to worsening | TTD | TDD | Time to HRQoL deterioration | Symptom deterioration endpoint
Example_In_Context: The experimental arm demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in TTD for global health status (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.54–0.86, p=0.001) compared with standard of care, and this finding was included in the product label.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Kluetz PG et al. 2016 (Clin Cancer Res)

Short_Definition: Time to confirmed, sustained PRO worsening not followed by recovery above the deterioration threshold.
Extended_Definition: TTDD is a more stringent variant of TTD requiring that the observed deterioration be confirmed at one or more subsequent scheduled assessments and not subsequently recovered above the threshold. This confirmation requirement filters out transient symptom fluctuations and measurement noise, producing a more robust and reproducible endpoint. TTDD is analysed using the same survival analysis framework as TTD, but the event definition incorporates a confirmation window (e.g., two consecutive post-deterioration assessments below threshold). EMA has expressed preference for TTDD over TTD in oncology PRO analyses precisely because it distinguishes persistent from temporary worsening. In myeloma studies, TTDD is commonly applied to global health status, fatigue, and pain subscales of the EORTC QLQ-C30.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: TTDD is a more conservative and regulatorily defensible PRO endpoint than TTD, reducing false events that would bias time-to-event estimates. EMA reviewers increasingly expect TTDD as the primary or co-primary PRO endpoint in confirmatory oncology submissions.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Definitive deterioration | Confirmed deterioration | Sustained deterioration | Confirmed TTD | Time to confirmed worsening | Time to irreversible deterioration | TTDD | Persistent deterioration endpoint | Confirmed PRO worsening
Example_In_Context: TTDD was defined as a ≥10-point decline in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status confirmed at two consecutive assessments, with a median TTDD of 12.4 months in the control arm versus not reached in the experimental arm (HR 0.61, p=0.004).
Source: EMA Reflection Paper on Methodological Issues in PRO Endpoints in Oncology [GUIDANCE] | Coens C et al. 2020 (Lancet Oncol)

Short_Definition: Time from randomisation to first PRO score improvement meeting a predefined meaningful threshold.
Extended_Definition: TTI measures the interval from baseline to the first occasion a patient's PRO score improves by at least the MID or another pre-specified threshold, analysed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards methods. Patients who never achieve the improvement threshold are censored at their last observation. TTI is used to characterise the speed and probability of onset of patient-perceived benefit from treatment, complementing TTD by defining the other temporal boundary of the patient experience arc. It is particularly relevant in symptom-burden-heavy diseases such as multiple myeloma, where early pain or fatigue relief is a meaningful and differentiating clinical goal. Sensitivity analyses typically vary the improvement threshold and censoring assumptions.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: TTI captures treatment benefit onset from the patient's perspective, which is distinct from clinical response endpoints and directly supports labelling language about early symptomatic relief. In MM, rapid TTI for pain or fatigue can differentiate regimens with similar PFS profiles.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Time to PRO improvement | Time to symptom improvement | Time to first improvement | Time to meaningful improvement | Time to HRQoL improvement | TTI | Onset of symptomatic benefit | Time to patient-reported response
Example_In_Context: Median TTI for pain intensity was 6.1 weeks (95% CI 4.3–8.2) in the daratumumab-based regimen, significantly shorter than the 14.5 weeks observed in the comparator arm (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.42–0.72, p<0.001).
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Common usage in regulatory literature

Short_Definition: Ratio of event hazard rates between treatment and control groups over study follow-up.
Extended_Definition: The hazard ratio is the primary summary statistic from Cox proportional hazards regression, representing the ratio of the instantaneous rate of an event (e.g., PRO deterioration) in the treatment group relative to the control group at any given moment. An HR < 1 favours the treatment group (lower event rate); HR > 1 favours control; HR = 1 indicates equivalence. The proportional hazards assumption — that the HR remains constant over time — must be verified, as it can be violated in settings with delayed treatment effects or crossing survival curves. The HR is always reported with 95% confidence intervals and a p-value to convey statistical precision and significance. In PRO time-to-event analyses (TTD, TTDD, TTI), the HR quantifies how much a treatment reduces or increases the rate of symptom worsening or improvement.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: HR is the primary effect measure for all PRO time-to-event endpoints; its point estimate and CI directly determine whether a PRO-based labelling claim is statistically supportable and clinically informative. An AI agent must pair HR interpretation with proportional hazards verification and CI width assessment.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: HR | Hazard ratio | Cox HR | Relative hazard | Event rate ratio | Instantaneous risk ratio | Cox regression output | Exponentiated beta coefficient | Risk ratio (time-to-event)
Example_In_Context: The hazard ratio for time to deterioration in global health status was 0.72 (95% CI 0.58–0.89, p=0.003), indicating a 28% reduction in the risk of PRO deterioration with the experimental regimen.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Statistical Guidance on Clinical Trial Endpoints [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Smallest PRO score change considered meaningful to patients in a given clinical context.
Extended_Definition: The MID (also termed MCID) is the smallest difference in a PRO instrument score that patients perceive as noticeable and which would reasonably prompt a change in clinical management or patient decision-making. It is estimated using anchor-based methods — correlating PRO change scores with an external meaningful anchor such as a patient global impression of change rating — and/or distribution-based methods such as 0.5 SD or 1 standard error of measurement (SEM) of the baseline score. Regulatory agencies, including FDA, prefer anchor-based MIDs because they ground the threshold in patient perception rather than statistical distribution. The MID is instrument-specific, population-specific, and may differ for improvement versus deterioration directions. In multiple myeloma, MIDs have been established for EORTC QLQ-C30 (e.g., 10 points for global health status), FACT-MM, and BPI.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The MID is the conceptual anchor of all threshold-based PRO endpoints: it defines what counts as a TTD event, who qualifies as a responder, and whether a mean treatment difference is clinically meaningful. Without a validated, population-appropriate MID, PRO-based labelling claims are unlikely to be accepted by regulators.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: MID | MCID | Minimal clinically important difference | Minimal important difference | Clinically important difference | CID | Meaningful change threshold | Responder threshold | MID threshold | Within-patient meaningful change threshold | PRO threshold | Anchor-based MID | Distribution-based MID
Example_In_Context: A 10-point change on the EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status scale was used as the MID-based threshold to define deterioration events in the primary TTD analysis, per published anchor-based estimates in myeloma populations.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Revicki DA et al. 2008 (Health Qual Life Outcomes) | Cocks K et al. 2011 (Eur J Cancer)

Short_Definition: Likelihood-based longitudinal model analysing all PRO timepoints while handling missing data without imputation.
Extended_Definition: MMRM is a likelihood-based mixed-effects regression model applied to longitudinal PRO data that simultaneously estimates treatment effects across all scheduled assessment visits while accounting for within-patient correlation over time. It uses all available observed data from each patient — including those with incomplete follow-up — under the missing at random (MAR) assumption, without requiring explicit imputation of missing values. The model typically specifies fixed effects for treatment arm, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, and baseline PRO score as a covariate, combined with an unstructured or structured residual covariance matrix for the repeated measures. MMRM produces least-squares mean estimates and treatment differences at each timepoint, along with tests of overall treatment effect across visits. FDA and EMA consider MMRM the preferred primary analysis for continuous PRO outcomes in confirmatory oncology trials.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: MMRM is the regulatory gold standard for analysing continuous PRO trajectories over time, producing unbiased estimates under MAR and capturing the full longitudinal patient experience. It directly supports labelling claims about sustained HRQoL benefit or preservation across treatment duration.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: MMRM | Mixed model repeated measures | Mixed effects model for repeated measures | Linear mixed model | LMM | Longitudinal mixed model | REML model | Mixed model analysis | Repeated measures ANCOVA | MMRM analysis
Example_In_Context: The primary MMRM analysis demonstrated a statistically significant least-squares mean treatment difference of 5.3 points (95% CI 2.1–8.5, p=0.002) in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status at week 24, with treatment arm, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, and baseline score as model terms.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Mallinckrodt CH et al. 2008 (J Biopharm Stat) | NRC Report on Missing Data in Clinical Trials (2010) [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Missing data imputation substituting a patient's last observed PRO value for all subsequent missing assessments.
Extended_Definition: LOCF is a single imputation strategy in which the last recorded PRO score for each patient is substituted for all subsequent missing timepoints, treating it as if no change occurred after dropout. It was historically common in clinical trials due to simplicity and ease of regulatory acceptance, but it is now recognised as problematic because it can introduce systematic bias. In progressive diseases like multiple myeloma, where patients who deteriorate are more likely to drop out, LOCF carries forward a relatively good score for patients who subsequently worsened, artificially inflating treatment benefit estimates. FDA guidance explicitly discourages LOCF as a primary analysis method for PRO data, recommending model-based approaches (MMRM) or multiple imputation instead. LOCF retains a role in pre-specified sensitivity analyses with appropriate justification.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: LOCF can systematically bias PRO treatment effect estimates in oncology by underestimating the degree of symptom worsening in patients who drop out — a critical concern for regulatory credibility of PRO labelling claims. An AI agent should flag LOCF as primary analysis and flag whether dropout patterns are informative.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: LOCF | Last observation carried forward | Last value carried forward | LVCF | Single imputation | Carry-forward imputation | Last value imputation | Baseline observation carried forward (BOCF, related) | Single imputation method
Example_In_Context: Sensitivity analyses using LOCF showed attenuated treatment differences compared with the primary MMRM analysis, consistent with the expectation that LOCF underestimates deterioration in patients who discontinued due to progressive disease.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Missing Data in Clinical Trials (2019) [GUIDANCE] | NRC Report on Prevention and Treatment of Missing Data in Clinical Studies (2010) [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Categorical analysis classifying patients as PRO responders or non-responders based on MID-threshold score change.
Extended_Definition: Responder analysis converts continuous PRO score changes into binary or ordinal categories — typically improvement, stability, and deterioration — by applying a predefined MID-based threshold to each patient's change from baseline. This approach enhances clinical interpretability by communicating the proportion of patients who experienced a meaningful benefit, rather than reporting only mean score differences that can be difficult for clinicians and patients to interpret. Results are presented as proportions with confidence intervals, odds ratios, or risk differences, and may be visualised using cumulative distribution function (CDF) plots across the full spectrum of score changes. FDA guidance recommends responder analyses as a complement to continuous MMRM analyses to support labelling language about meaningful symptom benefit. Sensitivity analyses should explore multiple thresholds to assess robustness.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Responder analysis translates PRO data into clinically communicable proportions, directly enabling labelling language such as "X% of patients reported meaningful improvement in symptoms." It is the key bridge between statistical PRO results and patient-facing benefit claims in regulatory submissions.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Responder analysis | Categorical analysis | MID-based responder analysis | Clinical responder analysis | Binary responder analysis | Threshold-based analysis | Proportion responding | CDF plot | Cumulative distribution function analysis | Patient-level response analysis | Response rate (PRO)
Example_In_Context: Responder analysis showed that 61% of patients in the experimental arm achieved a ≥10-point improvement in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status at week 16, compared with 38% in the control arm (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.74–3.73, p<0.001).
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Cella D et al. 2002 (J Clin Oncol) | Revicki DA et al. 2006 (Pharmacoeconomics)

Short_Definition: PRO score change that exceeds the MID and is perceptible and practically significant to patients or clinicians.
Extended_Definition: Clinically meaningful change refers to a difference in PRO score that exceeds the validated MID threshold and therefore represents a change that patients would notice, that has practical implications for well-being or clinical management, and that is not merely a statistical artefact. It is conceptually distinct from statistical significance: a change can be statistically significant in a large trial yet fall below the MID and thus lack clinical meaningfulness — and vice versa in small samples. The concept applies both at the individual patient level (did this patient's score change meaningfully?) and the group level (did the treatment produce a meaningful average difference?). Regulatory agencies require sponsors to contextualise PRO findings in terms of clinical meaningfulness before granting labelling claims, typically by anchoring results to validated MIDs. In multiple myeloma submissions, clinical meaningfulness is assessed for instruments including EORTC QLQ-C30, FACT-MM, and BPI-SF.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Demonstrating clinical meaningfulness — not merely statistical significance — is a prerequisite for PRO-based labelling claims. An AI agent must distinguish statistically significant but clinically trivial PRO differences from genuinely meaningful changes, particularly in large trials where small effects achieve significance.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Clinically meaningful change | Clinical meaningfulness | Clinically significant change | Meaningful change | Patient-meaningful change | Clinically important change | Substantial symptomatic benefit | Within-patient meaningful change | MID-exceeding change | PRO clinical significance
Example_In_Context: Although the treatment arm showed a statistically significant mean improvement of 3.2 points on the fatigue subscale (p=0.03), this fell below the 10-point MID threshold and was therefore not characterised as clinically meaningful in the regulatory submission.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Revicki DA et al. 2008 (Health Qual Life Outcomes) | Jaeschke R et al. 1989 (Control Clin Trials)

Short_Definition: Standardised, scale-free measure of the magnitude of difference between two groups.
Extended_Definition: Effect size quantifies the practical magnitude of a treatment difference in standardised units independent of sample size, enabling comparisons across instruments and studies. Common metrics in PRO research include Cohen's d (mean difference divided by pooled SD), Glass's delta (divided by control SD), Hedges' g (bias-corrected d), and the standardised response mean (SRM, mean change divided by SD of change). By convention, effect sizes of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 are considered small, medium, and large respectively, though these benchmarks require contextualisation with instrument-specific MIDs. Distribution-based MID estimation frequently uses 0.5 SD or 1 SEM as approximations, directly linking effect size metrics to MID derivation. Effect sizes facilitate cross-trial synthesis and meta-analysis of PRO data across heterogeneous instruments.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Effect size allows an AI agent to benchmark PRO treatment differences against conventions and across studies using different instruments, supporting cross-trial comparison and meta-analysis. It is especially valuable when comparing MM trials that use different PRO instruments with different scale ranges.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Effect size | Cohen's d | Standardised mean difference | SMD | Glass's delta | Hedges' g | Standardised response mean | SRM | d-statistic | PRO effect magnitude | Normalised treatment difference
Example_In_Context: The treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-C30 physical functioning corresponded to Cohen's d = 0.48, indicating a medium effect size that approached but did not exceed the distribution-based MID approximation of 0.5 SD.
Source: Cohen J 1988 (Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences) | Wyrwich KW et al. 1999 (J Clin Epidemiol) | Norman GR et al. 2003 (Med Care)

Short_Definition: Range of plausible values for an estimated parameter at a specified probability level, typically 95%.
Extended_Definition: A confidence interval provides a range of values within which the true population parameter (e.g., mean treatment difference, HR, odds ratio) is estimated to lie with a specified level of confidence, most commonly 95%. The correct interpretation is frequentist: if the study were repeated many times under identical conditions, 95% of the computed intervals would contain the true parameter value — it is not the probability that the true value lies in any single interval. For PRO analyses, CIs around mean score differences, hazard ratios, and responder proportions are essential for assessing the precision and practical significance of treatment effects. Narrow CIs indicate high precision; wide CIs signal uncertainty, typically due to small sample size, high PRO score variability, or high dropout rates. Regulatory reviewers assess CIs alongside p-values to evaluate both statistical significance and the plausible range of effect sizes.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: CIs communicate the precision of PRO treatment effect estimates, directly affecting regulatory confidence in labelling claims. An AI agent should flag wide CIs — particularly when the lower bound falls below the MID — as indicating insufficient precision to support robust PRO conclusions.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: CI | Confidence interval | 95% CI | 90% CI | 99% CI | Interval estimate | Uncertainty interval | Precision interval | Frequentist CI | Bayesian credible interval (CrI, related) | Two-sided CI | One-sided CI
Example_In_Context: The mean treatment difference in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status was 6.8 points (95% CI 3.2–10.4), with the lower CI bound exceeding the 3-point distribution-based MID, supporting a claim of clinically meaningful improvement.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Probability of observing results as extreme as the data assuming the null hypothesis is true.
Extended_Definition: The p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the observed value, given that the null hypothesis of no treatment effect is true. A p-value below a pre-specified significance threshold (α = 0.05 two-sided, or α = 0.025 one-sided, in most Phase III trials) is used to declare statistical significance. Critically, a p-value does not measure the probability that the null hypothesis is true, the magnitude of the treatment effect, or the clinical importance of the finding. In PRO analyses involving multiple domains or timepoints, unadjusted p-values are highly susceptible to multiplicity inflation; pre-specified hierarchical testing procedures or alpha adjustment methods (e.g., Bonferroni, Hochberg) are required for confirmatory analyses. Regulatory agencies require that alpha levels and multiplicity control strategies be pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: P-values gatekeep whether PRO endpoints achieve the statistical significance required for confirmatory labelling claims, but their interpretation requires multiplicity control and contextualisation with effect size and CIs. An AI agent must flag unadjusted p-values, absent testing hierarchies, and situations where significance is achieved without clinical meaningfulness.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: p-value | p value | P | Significance level | Alpha | Statistical significance | Nominal p-value | Adjusted p-value | Unadjusted p-value | Two-sided p-value | One-sided p-value | Observed significance level | Type I error | Alpha threshold
Example_In_Context: The pre-specified hierarchical testing procedure controlled the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05; the primary PRO endpoint of TTD achieved p = 0.003 and was considered confirmatory, while secondary HRQoL domain comparisons were tested sequentially without further alpha adjustment.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | Wasserstein RL & Lazar NA 2016 (Am Stat)

Short_Definition: An endpoint formally defined in the protocol or SAP before any unblinded data are examined.
Extended_Definition: A prespecified endpoint is any outcome measure, analysis method, threshold, or hypothesis formally documented in the trial protocol or statistical analysis plan (SAP) prior to database lock or unblinding, establishing it as an a priori commitment rather than a post-hoc observation. Prespecification must cover the endpoint definition, instrument, scoring algorithm, MID threshold, timepoint, analysis method, and multiplicity position to be considered fully prespecified by regulatory standards. FDA and EMA require that PRO labelling claims be based exclusively on prespecified endpoints; findings arising from analyses not prespecified are considered hypothesis-generating only. The regulatory rationale is to prevent outcome reporting bias and selective analysis, which inflate Type I error rates. For PRO submissions in multiple myeloma, the SAP must explicitly state whether TTD, TTDD, or domain-specific analyses are confirmatory or exploratory prior to any unblinding.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Prespecification is a binary gatekeeping criterion for regulatory credibility: only prespecified PRO endpoints can support confirmatory labelling claims. An AI agent must classify every PRO finding as prespecified or not and escalate the distinction when evaluating regulatory strength of evidence.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Prespecified endpoint | Pre-specified endpoint | A priori endpoint | Protocol-specified endpoint | SAP-defined endpoint | Pre-planned analysis | Pre-registered endpoint | Confirmatory prespecified endpoint | Primary prespecified endpoint | Secondary prespecified endpoint | Protocol amendment endpoint
Example_In_Context: The TTD for pain intensity was a prespecified secondary endpoint in the SAP filed on 14 March 2021, prior to database lock, and therefore supported a confirmatory interpretation in the regulatory submission.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | ICH E9(R1) Addendum on Estimands (2019) [GUIDANCE]

Term: Alpha Control / Type I Error Control
Short_Definition: Procedures that maintain the probability of falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis at or below a prespecified level.
Extended_Definition: Type I error is the probability of incorrectly concluding a treatment effect exists when the null hypothesis is actually true; alpha (α) is the prespecified maximum acceptable Type I error rate, conventionally set at 0.05 (two-sided) or 0.025 (one-sided) in confirmatory Phase III trials. When multiple endpoints or hypotheses are tested within a single trial — as is common in PRO-inclusive oncology trials — the family-wise error rate (FWER) inflates above α unless formal control procedures are applied. Alpha control methods include Bonferroni correction, Holm-step-down, Hochberg step-up, fixed-sequence hierarchical testing, and graphical testing procedures such as the Maurer-Bretz approach. Regulatory agencies require FWER control at the 0.05 level across all confirmatory primary and key secondary endpoints, including PRO endpoints included in the confirmatory testing hierarchy. Without documented alpha control, PRO findings cannot support label claims regardless of p-value magnitude.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Alpha control determines whether any PRO endpoint can achieve confirmatory regulatory status; without it, statistically significant PRO results remain exploratory. An AI agent must verify that PRO endpoints in submissions are positioned within a multiplicity-controlled testing strategy before attributing confirmatory weight.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Alpha control | Type I error control | FWER | Family-wise error rate | Alpha inflation | Multiple comparison problem | Multiplicity control | Significance threshold | Alpha level | Experiment-wise error rate | Bonferroni | Holm procedure | Hochberg procedure | Graphical testing procedure | Confirmatory alpha
Example_In_Context: To control the family-wise error rate at 0.05, a hierarchical testing procedure was applied: PFS was tested first, followed by OS, with TTD for global health status tested only if both PFS and OS achieved statistical significance.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials Guidance (2022) [GUIDANCE] | Bretz F et al. 2009 (Biometrical J)

Short_Definition: Sequential hypothesis testing procedure where secondary endpoints are tested only if primary endpoints achieve significance.
Extended_Definition: Hierarchical testing (also called sequential or fixed-sequence testing) is a multiplicity control strategy in which endpoints are ordered by clinical and regulatory priority, and each endpoint is tested at the full alpha level only if all preceding endpoints in the hierarchy have achieved statistical significance. If any endpoint in the sequence fails to reach significance, all subsequent tests are declared non-significant and confirmatory testing stops. This procedure controls the FWER strongly without requiring alpha splitting, thereby preserving full power for each individual test within the hierarchy. PRO endpoints in oncology trials are typically positioned below survival endpoints (PFS, OS) in the hierarchy, meaning PRO confirmation depends on those upstream endpoints achieving significance first. In multiple myeloma trials, a common hierarchy is: PFS → OS → TTD (global health status) → TTD (pain) → domain-specific subscales.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Hierarchical testing determines whether PRO endpoints can ever achieve confirmatory status in a given trial, as failure of upstream clinical endpoints forecloses PRO labelling claims regardless of PRO results. An AI agent must map the full testing hierarchy and identify where PRO endpoints sit to assess their confirmatory versus exploratory status.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Hierarchical testing | Sequential testing | Fixed-sequence testing | Step-down testing | Gatekeeper testing | Testing hierarchy | Serial gatekeeper | Primary-secondary testing cascade | Fixed-sequence procedure | Testing order | Gatekeeping procedure
Example_In_Context: Under the prespecified hierarchical testing procedure, PFS (p<0.001) and OS (p=0.018) both achieved significance, enabling confirmatory testing of TTD for global health status, which also reached significance (p=0.004) and supported a PRO labelling claim.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials Guidance (2022) [GUIDANCE] | Dmitrienko A & D'Agostino RB 2013 (N Engl J Med)

Short_Definition: Statistical corrections applied to significance thresholds when multiple hypotheses are tested to control false positive rates.
Extended_Definition: Multiplicity adjustment encompasses any statistical method that modifies individual test significance thresholds or p-values to account for the increased probability of at least one false positive when multiple hypotheses are tested simultaneously within a single trial. Specific adjustment approaches include Bonferroni (divide α by number of tests), Holm step-down, Hochberg step-up, Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) control, and graphical procedures that distribute alpha across families of endpoints. Multiplicity is relevant in PRO contexts at three levels: across multiple PRO endpoints, across multiple PRO domains within an instrument, and across multiple assessment timepoints for a single domain. FDA guidance for oncology trials requires explicit multiplicity adjustment for all confirmatory PRO analyses; exploratory PRO analyses may report unadjusted p-values if clearly labelled. Failure to adequately address multiplicity in a PRO submission is a common FDA and EMA deficiency finding.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Multiplicity adjustment directly governs which PRO findings receive confirmatory status in regulatory review; inadequate adjustment is a leading reason PRO claims are rejected or downgraded to exploratory. An AI agent should flag any multi-domain or multi-timepoint PRO analysis that lacks a documented adjustment strategy.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Multiplicity adjustment | Multiple comparison adjustment | Bonferroni correction | Holm correction | Hochberg correction | FDR control | False discovery rate | Alpha adjustment | Multiple testing correction | Adjusted p-value | Familywise correction | Type I error adjustment | Multiple endpoints correction
Example_In_Context: Multiplicity was addressed by applying the Hochberg step-up procedure to the four PRO secondary endpoints, maintaining the family-wise error rate at 0.05; two of the four endpoints achieved adjusted significance, supporting their inclusion in the product label.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Multiple Endpoints in Clinical Trials Guidance (2022) [GUIDANCE] | Hochberg Y 1988 (Biometrika)

Short_Definition: Approved language in a product's prescribing information describing a demonstrated treatment benefit.
Extended_Definition: A label claim is the specific text included in the approved prescribing information (United States Package Insert, USPI; or Summary of Product Characteristics, SmPC) that describes a clinically and statistically substantiated treatment benefit, including those derived from PRO data. PRO-based label claims typically describe symptomatic benefit, health-related quality of life preservation, or delay of symptom worsening, and require evidence from prespecified, multiplicity-controlled, confirmatory analyses supported by validated instruments. FDA distinguishes between claims that appear in the Indications and Usage section (requiring highest evidence standard) versus those in Clinical Studies or Patient Counselling Information sections (somewhat lower threshold). The precise wording, strength, and positioning of a PRO claim are negotiated between the sponsor and the regulatory agency during the review process and are directly influenced by data quality, instrument validation, and missing data management. In multiple myeloma, PRO label claims have been achieved for pain, fatigue, and global health status for several approved therapies.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Label claims are the ultimate translational output of PRO data in regulatory submissions — they are the mechanism by which patient-centred evidence reaches prescribers, payers, and patients. An AI agent assessing PRO programmes should evaluate every analysis against the evidentiary standard required for the type of label claim the sponsor intends to pursue.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Label claim | Labelling claim | PRO label claim | Prescribing information claim | Package insert claim | USPI claim | SmPC claim | Symptom claim | HRQoL claim | Approved claim | Regulatory claim | Indications and Usage claim | Clinical Studies section claim | Patient Counselling Information claim
Example_In_Context: Following the confirmatory TTD analysis demonstrating a 32% reduction in risk of global health status deterioration, FDA approved a label claim in the Clinical Studies section stating that the treatment delayed deterioration in patient-reported global health status compared with standard of care.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | FDA Guidance on Labeling for Human Prescription Drug and Biological Products [GUIDANCE] | Kluetz PG et al. 2016 (Clin Cancer Res)

Short_Definition: An endpoint analysed without multiplicity control, intended to generate hypotheses rather than confirmatory evidence.
Extended_Definition: An exploratory endpoint is any endpoint not positioned within the confirmatory multiplicity-controlled testing hierarchy — either because it was prespecified as exploratory in the SAP or because it was added, modified, or conducted post-hoc after data unblinding. Exploratory analyses are conducted without formal alpha control, meaning their p-values are unadjusted nominal values that do not provide confirmatory evidence of treatment effect. They serve to generate scientific hypotheses, assess internal consistency of findings, and identify signals for future trial design, but cannot support regulatory label claims on their own. In PRO-inclusive oncology trials, exploratory endpoints may include subgroup HRQoL analyses, individual PRO domain trajectories, or novel instruments not yet validated for the target population. FDA and EMA require that exploratory endpoints be clearly labelled as such in submissions to prevent misinterpretation of nominal significance as confirmatory evidence.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Exploratory PRO endpoints contribute to the scientific narrative and hypothesis generation but cannot be used by an AI agent to attribute confirmed treatment benefit. Distinguishing exploratory from confirmatory PRO results is one of the highest-value classification tasks in regulatory PRO document analysis.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Exploratory endpoint | Exploratory analysis | Hypothesis-generating analysis | Nominal analysis | Unadjusted analysis | Non-confirmatory endpoint | Descriptive endpoint | Supportive PRO analysis | Signal-detection analysis | Pilot endpoint | Tertiary endpoint
Example_In_Context: Domain-specific analyses of physical functioning, emotional functioning, and fatigue were prespecified as exploratory endpoints; although all three showed numerical improvement favouring the experimental arm, these results were characterised as hypothesis-generating and did not contribute to the confirmatory PRO evidence package.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | ICH E9(R1) Addendum on Estimands (2019) [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: The evidentiary standard required by FDA for approval of a drug's effectiveness, typically from adequate and well-controlled trials.
Extended_Definition: Substantial evidence is the statutory standard under the US Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (Section 505) that FDA requires to approve a drug or biological product, defined as evidence from adequate and well-controlled investigations by qualified scientific experts showing the drug will have the claimed effect. For PRO-based label claims, substantial evidence requires that findings come from at least one — and typically two — adequate and well-controlled trials with prespecified, multiplicity-adjusted, confirmatory PRO endpoints analysed with validated instruments and appropriate missing data management. The standard is higher for claims in the Indications and Usage section than for descriptive findings in the Clinical Studies section. FDA's Oncology Center of Excellence has acknowledged that a single well-controlled trial with highly persuasive PRO results may meet the substantial evidence threshold in some oncology contexts. In practice, substantial evidence for a PRO claim requires the convergence of statistical significance, clinical meaningfulness, instrument validity, and absence of major data quality concerns.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The substantial evidence standard defines the ceiling of evidentiary quality an AI agent must assess PRO data against to determine whether label claim language is likely to be approved versus rejected. It is the operative standard for all confirmatory PRO endpoint evaluation in US regulatory submissions.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Substantial evidence | Adequate and well-controlled evidence | Confirmatory evidence | Regulatory evidence standard | Proof of effectiveness | Pivotal evidence | FD&C Act Section 505 standard | Two-trial standard | Single persuasive trial standard | Strong evidence | Level of evidence
Example_In_Context: FDA reviewers concluded that the single pivotal trial, while providing substantial evidence of PFS benefit, did not independently meet the substantial evidence standard for the PRO label claim owing to high PRO missing data rates exceeding 20% at the primary timepoint.
Source: US Food Drug and Cosmetic Act Section 505 [GUIDANCE] | FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | FDA Guidance: Demonstrating Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness (2019) [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Evidence that corroborates but does not independently establish a treatment effect or label claim.
Extended_Definition: Supportive evidence refers to data that reinforce, contextualize, or add plausibility to a primary finding but that, on their own, would not meet the substantial evidence threshold for a regulatory claim. In PRO submissions, supportive evidence may include exploratory domain analyses, subgroup PRO findings, responder proportions accompanying a primary MMRM result, or PRO data from a second trial in a different line of therapy. The distinction between supportive and confirmatory evidence is critically dependent on prespecification and multiplicity control: a finding that is statistically significant but exploratory is supportive, not confirmatory. FDA frequently requests supportive PRO analyses to build a coherent benefit-risk narrative around a primary survival endpoint even when PRO data alone are insufficient for a standalone label claim. Supportive PRO evidence is often presented in the Clinical Studies section of the label rather than the Indications and Usage section.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Supportive PRO evidence shapes the overall benefit-risk narrative presented to prescribers and health technology assessment bodies, even when it cannot independently sustain a label claim. An AI agent should classify and weight PRO findings as confirmatory or supportive, as this distinction determines how they are used in benefit-risk argumentation.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Supportive evidence | Corroborating evidence | Supplementary evidence | Secondary evidence | Non-confirmatory evidence | Contextual evidence | Complementary evidence | Descriptive supportive data | Exploratory supportive evidence | HRQoL supportive data
Example_In_Context: While the PRO analyses in the phase II trial were considered supportive evidence given the smaller sample size and absence of multiplicity control, they were included in the integrated summary of efficacy to contextualise the phase III findings and support the benefit-risk discussion.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | EMA Appendix 2 to the Guideline on the Evaluation of Anticancer Medicinal Products in Man [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: An unplanned analysis conducted after data unblinding, not prespecified in the protocol or SAP.
Extended_Definition: A post-hoc analysis is any analysis not prespecified in the trial protocol or SAP prior to unblinding, conducted after examination of the data has begun or after the primary analysis has been completed. Post-hoc analyses are inherently hypothesis-generating because they capitalise on chance findings in the observed data, inflating the probability of spurious conclusions and precluding formal Type I error control. In PRO research, common post-hoc analyses include subgroup HRQoL comparisons, novel threshold definitions applied retrospectively, and additional domain analyses beyond those in the SAP. Regulatory agencies do not accept post-hoc PRO analyses as confirmatory evidence for label claims; they may, however, be submitted as exploratory or supportive data with clear labelling of their unplanned nature. Transparency in reporting — explicitly distinguishing post-hoc from prespecified analyses — is required by regulatory guidance and expected in journal submissions.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Post-hoc PRO analyses are the lowest tier of evidentiary weight in regulatory evaluation and must be clearly flagged by an AI agent to prevent erroneous attribution of confirmatory status. Failure to distinguish post-hoc from prespecified findings is a critical analytical error in regulatory document review.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Post-hoc analysis | Post hoc analysis | Unplanned analysis | Data-driven analysis | Retrospective analysis | Ad hoc analysis | Exploratory post-hoc | Hypothesis-generating analysis | Data-dredging | Outcome switching | Undisclosed analysis | Unprespecified analysis
Example_In_Context: The sponsor noted that the subgroup analysis of TTD in patients aged >65 years was a post-hoc analysis not prespecified in the SAP, and therefore characterised the numerically superior HR of 0.61 as hypothesis-generating, to be tested prospectively in a dedicated trial.
Source: ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials [GUIDANCE] | FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Altman DG & Bland JM 1994 (BMJ)

Short_Definition: Repeated analyses under alternative assumptions to assess the robustness of a primary result.
Extended_Definition: A sensitivity analysis is a pre-planned or post-hoc replication of a primary analysis under alternative but plausible methodological assumptions, with the purpose of testing whether the primary conclusion holds under a range of conditions. In PRO analyses, sensitivity analyses commonly vary: the missing data handling method (e.g., MMRM vs. LOCF vs. multiple imputation), the deterioration threshold (±5 points around the primary MID), the censoring rules for TTD/TTDD, and the handling of patients who switch treatment. Sensitivity analyses must be distinguished from primary analyses in reporting, with their role explicitly framed as assessing robustness rather than providing independent confirmatory evidence. FDA guidance on missing data (2019) specifically requires pre-planned sensitivity analyses for any longitudinal PRO primary endpoint to address the MAR assumption underlying MMRM. Converging sensitivity analysis results strengthen regulatory confidence in the primary finding; divergent results prompt additional scrutiny and agency queries.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Sensitivity analyses are essential for demonstrating that PRO labelling claims are robust to methodological uncertainty — particularly missing data assumptions — which regulators view as a major threat to PRO data validity. An AI agent should evaluate the breadth, pre-specification, and convergence of sensitivity analyses when assessing the strength of a PRO evidence package.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Sensitivity analysis | Robustness analysis | Alternative analysis | Scenario analysis | Assumption testing | Missing data sensitivity | MNAR sensitivity | Tipping point analysis | Stress test analysis | Supplementary analysis | What-if analysis | Plausible assumption analysis
Example_In_Context: Pre-specified sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation under a missing-not-at-random (MNAR) assumption produced HR estimates ranging from 0.69 to 0.74 for TTD, consistent with the primary MMRM result of 0.71, confirming the robustness of the PRO finding.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Missing Data in Clinical Trials (2019) [GUIDANCE] | NRC Report on Prevention and Treatment of Missing Data in Clinical Studies (2010) [GUIDANCE] | ICH E9(R1) Addendum on Estimands (2019) [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: Regulatory approval granted with post-marketing obligations pending confirmatory evidence of clinical benefit.
Extended_Definition: Conditional approval (EMA) or Accelerated Approval (FDA) allows marketing authorisation for a drug based on surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoints reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, with a mandatory commitment to provide confirmatory evidence from ongoing or planned trials within a specified timeframe. In oncology, surrogate endpoints such as PFS, ORR, or MRD negativity may trigger conditional approval while OS and HRQoL data mature. Under FDA's Accelerated Approval programme, if confirmatory trials do not verify the predicted clinical benefit, the approval may be withdrawn. PRO data at the time of conditional approval are often exploratory or immature, but regulators may require sponsors to commit to PRO data collection and reporting in post-marketing studies to support full approval with HRQoL labelling claims. EMA's conditional approval framework explicitly lists PRO and HRQoL data among the outstanding measures that may be required for conversion to full approval.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Conditional approval creates a critical regulatory window where PRO data are often absent or preliminary; an AI agent must flag whether PRO endpoints are part of the confirmatory post-marketing commitment and track submission deadlines for PRO evidence required for full approval conversion.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Conditional approval | Accelerated Approval | Conditional marketing authorisation | CMA | AA | Provisional approval | Approval with conditions | Surrogate endpoint approval | Post-marketing commitment | Post-marketing requirement | PMR | PMC | Confirmatory post-marketing study | Restricted approval | Provisional marketing authorisation
Example_In_Context: At the time of conditional approval based on MRD negativity rate, PRO data from the pivotal trial were immature; the sponsor committed to submitting comprehensive EORTC QLQ-C30 TTD analyses from the final OS data cut as a post-marketing requirement to support conversion to full approval.
Source: FDA Accelerated Approval Regulations 21 CFR 314.510 [GUIDANCE] | EMA Guideline on Conditional Marketing Authorisation (2016) [GUIDANCE] | FDA Oncology Center of Excellence Accelerated Approval Guidance [GUIDANCE]

Short_Definition: A multidimensional patient-reported construct capturing physical, emotional, social, and functional well-being affected by disease and treatment.
Extended_Definition: HRQoL is a multidimensional construct encompassing the domains of physical functioning, emotional well-being, social functioning, role functioning, and symptomatic burden as perceived and reported by the patient in the context of their illness and its treatment. It is distinct from broader quality of life (QoL) concepts in that it specifically captures health-related dimensions, excluding aspects such as financial status or environmental satisfaction not directly mediated by disease or therapy. HRQoL is operationalised through validated self-report instruments — such as the EORTC QLQ-C30, FACT-G, EQ-5D, or disease-specific extensions — that aggregate patient responses into domain scores or global indices. FDA and EMA consider HRQoL a key patient-centred outcome in oncology drug development, and EMA's Appendix 2 guidance explicitly calls for HRQoL data collection in pivotal trials. In multiple myeloma, HRQoL is particularly important given the chronic, relapsing nature of the disease and the cumulative symptom burden imposed by successive treatment lines.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: HRQoL is the overarching construct that PRO instruments operationalise; it provides the conceptual framework within which all PRO domain and subscale findings are interpreted for regulatory submissions. An AI agent must map individual PRO instrument scores back to the HRQoL domains they represent to correctly characterise the scope and completeness of the patient-centred evidence package.

Example_In_Context: The primary HRQoL endpoint, EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status, showed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement of 8.2 points (95% CI 4.7–11.7, p<0.001) in the experimental arm at week 24, supporting the HRQoL label claim.

Short_Definition: Any report of a patient's health status coming directly from the patient without clinician interpretation.
Extended_Definition: A patient-reported outcome is any assessment of a patient's health condition that comes directly and solely from the patient, without interpretation or modification by a clinician or any other individual. PROs encompass symptoms, functional status, health-related quality of life, treatment satisfaction, and adherence, and are distinguished from clinician-reported outcomes (ClinROs), observer-reported outcomes (ObsROs), and performance outcomes (PerfOs) under the FDA Clinical Outcome Assessment (COA) taxonomy. The regulatory rationale for PROs is that certain aspects of patient experience — particularly symptom severity, emotional impact, and perceived functioning — cannot be validly inferred from clinical assessments alone and require direct patient input. FDA's 2009 PRO guidance established the foundational framework for using PRO measures to support labelling claims, emphasising instrument validation, conceptual framework development, and cognitive debriefing. In oncology, PROs have become increasingly central to benefit-risk assessment, particularly for symptomatic diseases such as multiple myeloma where treatment-related toxicity and disease burden are high.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: PRO is the foundational regulatory category that defines the scope and evidentiary standards of all patient-centred data in clinical submissions. An AI agent must accurately classify outcome data as PRO vs. ClinRO vs. ObsRO before applying appropriate validation, analysis, and evidentiary weight criteria.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: PRO | Patient-reported outcome | Patient reported outcome | Patient self-report | Self-reported outcome | Patient assessment | Direct patient report | Patient-centred outcome | COA | Clinical outcome assessment | PRO data | Patient-reported data | Self-assessed outcome
Example_In_Context: FDA's review of the NDA noted that the primary PRO endpoint — patient-reported pain intensity — was based on direct patient self-report using the BPI-SF, consistent with the definition of a PRO under the 2009 guidance, and was not subject to modification by site investigators.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | FDA Clinical Outcome Assessment Compendium [GUIDANCE] | Basch E et al. 2014 (J Clin Oncol)

Short_Definition: A validated questionnaire or instrument used to collect and quantify patient-reported outcome data.
Extended_Definition: A PRO measure is a standardised, validated instrument comprising one or more items through which patients report their health status, symptoms, or functioning; the instrument produces scored data that can be analysed statistically and interpreted clinically. PROMs range from generic instruments applicable across disease areas (e.g., EQ-5D, SF-36) to disease-specific tools (e.g., EORTC QLQ-MY20 for myeloma, FACT-MM) and symptom-specific scales (e.g., BPI-SF for pain, FACIT-Fatigue). Regulatory acceptance of a PROM requires documented evidence of content validity — typically through qualitative patient interviews and cognitive debriefing — as well as psychometric validation demonstrating reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness to change. FDA's 2009 PRO guidance outlines a detailed qualification pathway for PROMs intended to support label claims, including concept elicitation studies in the target patient population. The choice of PROM directly determines which concepts can be claimed in a label, as a PROM can only support claims for the concepts it was designed and validated to measure.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The PROM chosen for a trial determines the conceptual scope, psychometric credibility, and regulatory defensibility of the entire PRO evidence package. An AI agent must verify that the PROM used in a given analysis is validated for the specific patient population, disease stage, and concept of interest before treating its scores as regulatorily credible.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: PROM | PRO measure | PRO instrument | Patient-reported outcome measure | PRO questionnaire | PRO scale | PRO tool | Validated PRO | Patient questionnaire | Self-report measure | Health status instrument | PRO assessment tool | COA instrument

Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | EORTC Quality of Life Group QLQ-C30 Scoring Manual | Cella D et al. 1993 (J Clin Oncol)

Short_Definition: A distinct conceptual area of health or functioning measured by a subset of items within a PRO instrument.
Extended_Definition: A domain is a defined conceptual dimension of health, functioning, or symptom experience that a PRO instrument is designed to measure, represented by one or more items and scored as a distinct subscale or composite. In the EORTC QLQ-C30, for example, domains include physical functioning, role functioning, emotional functioning, cognitive functioning, social functioning, and global health status, alongside symptom scales for fatigue, pain, nausea, and dyspnoea. Domains are derived from a conceptual framework developed through qualitative patient research and should reflect concepts that patients identify as meaningful and distinct from one another. Regulatory submissions must explicitly identify which domains are primary versus secondary versus exploratory PRO endpoints and ensure each domain analysis is positioned appropriately in the multiplicity control hierarchy. Domain-level scores are distinct from total or global scores, and changes in individual domains may have different MIDs and regulatory interpretations.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Domain-level PRO analysis allows regulators and clinicians to understand which specific dimensions of patient experience a treatment impacts, enabling targeted and credible labelling language (e.g., "delays deterioration in pain" versus "improves overall HRQoL"). An AI agent must distinguish domain-level from total score analyses and cross-reference each domain to its validated MID and testing position.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Domain | PRO domain | HRQoL domain | Functional domain | Symptom domain | Scale | Subscale | Dimension | Concept | PRO concept | Facet | Health domain | Multi-domain | Domain score
Example_In_Context: Pre-specified analyses were conducted for five EORTC QLQ-C30 domains — physical functioning, fatigue, pain, global health status, and emotional functioning — with only global health status and pain positioned as confirmatory endpoints within the hierarchical testing procedure.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | EORTC QLQ-C30 Scoring Manual | Wilson IB & Cleary PD 1995 (JAMA)

Short_Definition: A scored grouping of related items within a PRO instrument measuring a single, coherent conceptual dimension.
Extended_Definition: A subscale is a scored composite of two or more instrument items that, together, measure a single coherent concept or domain within a PRO instrument; subscale scores are typically calculated as the mean or sum of constituent item responses, transformed to a 0–100 range where applicable. Subscales differ from total scores (aggregating all items) and single-item scales (individual questions), and each subscale may have its own MID, reliability estimate, and regulatory standing. Psychometric validation of a subscale includes internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha ≥0.70), test-retest reliability, convergent validity with related constructs, and discriminant validity from unrelated constructs. In regulatory submissions, subscale-level analyses must be prespecified and positioned in the multiplicity framework; reporting all subscale results without prior specification inflates Type I error. Subscale-level MIDs may differ from item-level or total score MIDs and must be established independently for each instrument-population combination.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Subscale scores are the primary unit of PRO analysis in most oncology trials, and their clinical interpretability depends on validated MIDs for each subscale in the specific disease population. An AI agent must pair every subscale result with its corresponding MID, psychometric validation status, and multiplicity position before assigning evidentiary weight.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Subscale | Sub-scale | PRO subscale | Domain score | Scale score | Component score | Composite score | Item cluster | Sub-domain | Dimensional score | Facet score | Module score
Example_In_Context: The EORTC QLQ-C30 fatigue subscale score at week 12 showed a mean improvement of 11.4 points (95% CI 6.8–16.0) in the experimental arm, exceeding the established 10-point MID for this subscale in myeloma patients and supporting the characterisation of a clinically meaningful reduction in fatigue.
Source: EORTC QLQ-C30 Scoring Manual | Osoba D et al. 1998 (J Clin Oncol) | Cocks K et al. 2011 (Eur J Cancer)

Short_Definition: A single preference-based index score representing overall health state value on a 0–1 scale anchored at death and full health.
Extended_Definition: A health utility score is a single summary index of overall health state derived from a preference-based instrument, anchored at 0 (dead) and 1 (full health), with negative values possible for health states considered worse than death. Utility scores are elicited using instruments such as the EQ-5D-3L, EQ-5D-5L, SF-6D, or HUI-3, which map patient responses through population-based value sets derived from preference elicitation exercises (e.g., time trade-off, standard gamble) in general population samples. Utility scores are the primary input for quality-adjusted life year (QALY) calculations used in health technology assessment (HTA) by bodies such as NICE, CADTH, and IQWIG. In multiple myeloma, utility scores are influenced by disease severity, treatment toxicity, and response depth, and may vary substantially across lines of therapy and health states. FDA does not typically require utility data for label approval, but HTA submissions require robust utility evidence to support reimbursement decisions.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Health utility scores bridge PRO data from clinical trials to health economic modelling, enabling QALY calculation and cost-effectiveness analysis for payer submissions. An AI agent operating across both regulatory and HTA contexts must distinguish utility-based instruments from non-preference-based PROMs and flag utility data as critical inputs for reimbursement evidence packages.

Example_In_Context: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility scores improved from 0.61 at baseline to 0.72 at week 24 in the experimental arm, a difference of 0.11 utility units exceeding the published MID of 0.07 for the EQ-5D-5L in haematological malignancies, and were used as health state inputs for the NICE cost-effectiveness model.
Source: EMA Guideline on the Clinical Investigation of Medicines for the Treatment of Multiple Myeloma [GUIDANCE] | NICE Methods Guide (2022) [GUIDANCE] | Pickard AS et al. 2007 (Med Care)

Short_Definition: The proportion of expected PRO assessments that were actually completed by enrolled patients at each timepoint.
Extended_Definition: Completion rate is calculated as the number of patients who completed a PRO assessment at a given scheduled timepoint divided by the number of patients who were alive, on study, and eligible to complete that assessment at that timepoint, expressed as a percentage. It is distinct from overall compliance rate (which may pool across timepoints) and must be reported separately at each scheduled assessment window to identify visit-specific patterns of non-completion. FDA and EMA consider completion rates of ≥80% at each timepoint a minimum acceptable threshold for PRO data to be considered reliable and interpretable for regulatory purposes; rates below this trigger scrutiny of potential non-random dropout and bias. Completion rates should be reported by treatment arm to detect differential dropout — unequal completion rates between arms are a major threat to the validity of PRO comparisons. In multiple myeloma trials, completion rates often decline at later visits due to disease progression, toxicity, and death, requiring careful censoring and missing data strategies.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Completion rates are the primary data quality metric for PRO assessments; rates below 80% at key timepoints may invalidate PRO labelling claims regardless of statistical significance. An AI agent must extract and flag per-timepoint, per-arm completion rates and cross-reference them against thresholds when evaluating PRO evidence quality.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Completion rate | Assessment completion | Questionnaire completion rate | PRO completion | Data completion rate | Response rate (PRO) | Item completion | Visit completion rate | Assessment return rate | Questionnaire return rate | Non-completion | Observed data rate
Example_In_Context: PRO completion rates exceeded 85% at all assessments through week 24 in both treatment arms, declining to 71% at week 48 in the control arm primarily due to disease progression-related discontinuation, which the sponsor addressed through a pre-specified sensitivity analysis under MNAR assumptions.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Kluetz PG et al. 2016 (Clin Cancer Res) | Efficace F et al. 2014 (J Clin Oncol)

Short_Definition: The loss of patients from PRO data collection over time due to dropout, withdrawal, death, or missed assessments.
Extended_Definition: Attrition refers to the progressive reduction in the number of patients contributing PRO data over the course of a trial, resulting from study withdrawal, treatment discontinuation, death, loss to follow-up, or non-compliance with assessment schedules. Attrition is a critical threat to the validity of longitudinal PRO analyses because it is rarely random: patients who deteriorate, experience toxicity, or progress are more likely to drop out, creating a systematic bias toward overestimation of treatment benefit in observed-case analyses. Attrition patterns must be characterised by treatment arm, reason for dropout, and timing relative to key clinical events to assess the plausibility of the missing-at-random (MAR) assumption underpinning MMRM analyses. High attrition rates — particularly differential attrition between arms — are among the most common reasons FDA and EMA express scepticism about PRO findings in oncology submissions. Attrition should be presented in CONSORT-style flow diagrams and summarised as an attrition table by visit and arm in regulatory submissions.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Differential attrition between treatment arms is one of the most serious threats to the internal validity of PRO comparative analyses, as it can systematically bias TTD, mean score, and responder proportion estimates. An AI agent must assess attrition rates, reasons, and differential patterns before attributing credibility to PRO treatment comparisons.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Attrition | Patient dropout | Dropout | Study withdrawal | PRO dropout | Loss to follow-up | Longitudinal attrition | Missing participants | Non-completion | Participant loss | Differential attrition | Informative dropout | Non-random dropout | Death-related attrition
Example_In_Context: Differential attrition was identified as a potential bias source: by week 32, 38% of control arm patients had discontinued PRO assessments compared with 19% in the experimental arm, with disease progression the primary reason in both arms, raising concern about informative dropout in the MMRM analysis.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Missing Data in Clinical Trials (2019) [GUIDANCE] | NRC Report on Prevention and Treatment of Missing Data (2010) [GUIDANCE] | Bell ML et al. 2013 (BMJ)

Short_Definition: The proportion of all scheduled PRO assessments completed across all enrolled patients and all planned timepoints.
Extended_Definition: Compliance rate is a summary metric representing the overall proportion of scheduled PRO assessments completed across all patients and timepoints in a trial, typically expressed as a percentage and reported by treatment arm. It aggregates completion across all visits and is therefore a less granular measure than per-timepoint completion rate, potentially masking visit-specific drops in data quality. Compliance encompasses both item-level completion (all items in the questionnaire answered) and visit-level completion (the questionnaire returned at the correct assessment window). In regulatory submissions, compliance rates are reported alongside completion rates to give reviewers a comprehensive picture of PRO data quality. A compliance rate above 80% overall, combined with per-timepoint completion rates above 80% at the primary assessment window, is generally considered acceptable by FDA and EMA for confirmatory PRO analysis.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Overall compliance rate is a headline data quality indicator that regulators use to make an initial assessment of PRO dataset reliability; rates below 80% may lead reviewers to question whether the dataset can support a labelling claim. An AI agent should distinguish compliance rate from completion rate and flag discrepancies that suggest particular visit windows were problematic.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Compliance rate | PRO compliance | Assessment compliance | Questionnaire compliance | Overall completion rate | Adherence rate (PRO) | Item response rate | Protocol adherence (PRO) | Data capture rate | Assessment adherence | PRO adherence
Example_In_Context: Overall PRO compliance was 87% in the experimental arm and 83% in the control arm across all scheduled assessments from baseline to week 48, with both arms meeting the pre-specified acceptability threshold of ≥80% required to conduct the primary confirmatory PRO analysis.
Source: FDA Guidance for Industry: Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (2009) [GUIDANCE] | Efficace F et al. 2014 (J Clin Oncol) | Common usage in regulatory literature

Short_Definition: PRO score observations that were scheduled but not collected, regardless of the reason for non-collection.
Extended_Definition: Missing data in PRO research refers to any scheduled PRO assessment or individual item response that was not collected from an eligible patient, encompassing item-level missingness (individual questions skipped), visit-level missingness (entire questionnaire not returned at a scheduled visit), and patient-level missingness (all data absent from a specific timepoint onwards). The missing data mechanism is classified as missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), or missing not at random (MNAR), with MNAR — where missingness is related to the unobserved outcome value itself — posing the greatest threat to validity and being the most plausible scenario in progressive oncology. FDA's 2019 missing data guidance requires sponsors to specify a primary analysis method under an explicitly stated missing data assumption, supplemented by pre-planned sensitivity analyses under alternative assumptions (e.g., MNAR delta-adjustment or tipping-point analysis). High rates of missing data — particularly when differential between arms and plausibly MNAR — are the leading reason FDA reviewers downgrade PRO evidence from confirmatory to supportive. In multiple myeloma, death and disease progression are major drivers of missing PRO data and must be handled explicitly in the estimand specification.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Missing PRO data is the single most consequential data quality problem in regulatory PRO submissions, as it threatens the validity of all longitudinal analyses under any analytic approach. An AI agent must characterise the extent, pattern, mechanism plausibility, and handling of missing data for every PRO endpoint before assigning evidentiary weight.

Example_In_Context: A tipping point sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the primary MMRM result for global health status TTD remained statistically significant unless the unobserved outcomes of patients with missing data in the experimental arm were assumed to be at least 18 points worse than observed, a scenario considered implausible given the clinical context.

Short_Definition: The level of detail and resolution at which PRO data are collected, stored, and analysed.
Extended_Definition: Data granularity in PRO research refers to the resolution at which data are captured across three dimensions: item level (individual question responses preserved separately), subscale level (items aggregated into domain scores), and total/global score level (full instrument summary). High granularity means retaining item-level data, enabling reconstruction of any scoring algorithm, investigation of differential item functioning, and post-hoc score recalculation if scoring conventions change. Regulatory submissions should ideally include item-level PRO data in clinical data repositories so that FDA or EMA reviewers can independently verify score calculations and explore alternative analyses. Temporal granularity — the frequency of PRO assessment — is equally important: daily electronic diary data provide higher resolution symptom trajectories than monthly clinic-visit questionnaires but introduce compliance and burden challenges. In multiple myeloma, data granularity considerations affect whether symptom dynamics during treatment cycles can be detected and whether worsening during treatment can be distinguished from post-discontinuation deterioration.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Data granularity determines what analyses are possible post-hoc and how transparently PRO findings can be audited by regulators; item-level data retention is increasingly expected in regulatory submissions to support independent score verification. An AI agent must assess whether data are available at sufficient granularity to support the analyses claimed, particularly when reviewing integrated summaries or meta-analyses.
Synonyms_And_Related_Terms: Data granularity | Item-level data | Item-level PRO | Raw PRO data | PRO data resolution | Scoring granularity | Assessment frequency | Temporal resolution | Daily diary data | ePRO granularity | PRO data detail | Level of aggregation | PRO data structure | Disaggregated data
Example_In_Context: The sponsor retained item-level EORTC QLQ-C30 response data in the CDISC CDASH dataset, enabling FDA reviewers to independently recalculate all subscale scores and verify the accuracy of the MID-based deterioration event definitions applied in the primary TTD analysis.

Short_Definition: The property of a PRO finding that exceeds the MID and represents a perceptible, practically significant change for patients.
Extended_Definition: Clinical meaningfulness is the determination that an observed PRO score change or treatment difference is large enough to be noticeable to patients and relevant to their daily functioning, well-being, or clinical management decisions — operationalised by exceeding a validated MID threshold. It is conceptually and analytically distinct from statistical significance: large trials can produce statistically significant PRO differences that fall below the MID and are therefore not clinically meaningful, while small trials may show clinically meaningful changes that fail to achieve significance due to insufficient power. Regulatory agencies require sponsors to explicitly demonstrate clinical meaningfulness — not merely statistical significance — before granting PRO-based labelling claims, typically by anchoring observed effects to validated, population-specific MIDs. Clinical meaningfulness must be assessed separately for group-mean differences (does the average treatment effect exceed the MID?), responder proportions (what percentage of patients achieved a meaningful individual change?), and time-to-event analyses (does the HR translate to a clinically meaningful delay in deterioration?). In multiple myeloma submissions, FDA reviewers routinely cross-reference reported PRO differences against published MIDs for EORTC QLQ-C30 subscales, FACT-MM, and BPI-SF.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Clinical meaningfulness is the bridge between statistical PRO results and regulatory acceptability for labelling claims; statistically significant but clinically trivial PRO differences are routinely rejected as a basis for labelling. An AI agent must apply MID-based thresholds to every PRO treatment difference and explicitly flag findings where significance is achieved without meaningfulness, or vice versa.

Short_Definition: The distinction between a PRO finding unlikely due to chance alone versus one that meaningfully matters to patients.
Extended_Definition: Statistical significance indicates that an observed PRO treatment difference is unlikely to have arisen by chance under the null hypothesis, as determined by a p-value falling below a pre-specified alpha threshold; it is a function of both the true effect size and the sample size. Clinical significance — or clinical meaningfulness — indicates that the observed difference meets or exceeds the MID and therefore represents a change that patients perceive and that has practical implications for their well-being or care decisions. The two concepts are independent: large trials can produce statistically significant but clinically trivial PRO effects, while small trials may yield clinically meaningful differences that fail to reach statistical significance. Regulatory agencies explicitly require both thresholds to be met for PRO-based labelling claims — statistical significance establishes that the effect is real, while clinical significance establishes that it matters. Reporting only p-values without reference to MIDs is a recognised deficiency in PRO submissions and a common agency query.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The statistical vs. clinical significance distinction is one of the most common sources of misinterpretation in PRO regulatory documents. An AI agent must apply both criteria simultaneously to every PRO treatment difference and flag findings where only one criterion is satisfied, as this directly determines whether a finding can support a labelling claim.

Example_In_Context: The independent data monitoring committee noted that the 3.8-point improvement in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status, while statistically significant (p=0.04), did not meet the pre-specified 10-point MID threshold, and recommended the finding be characterised as statistically significant but not clinically meaningful in the submission.
