Short_Definition: The absence of detectable residual myeloma cells at a prespecified sensitivity threshold by a validated molecular or immunophenotypic assay.
Extended_Definition: MRD negativity is defined as the failure to detect clonal myeloma plasma cells at or below a prespecified analytical sensitivity threshold — typically 10⁻⁵ or 10⁻⁶ — using a validated NGS or NGF assay in a bone marrow aspirate from a patient who has achieved at least CR by conventional IMWG criteria. The sensitivity threshold must be explicitly stated when reporting MRD negativity rates, as 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁶ negativity have different prognostic implications and are not interchangeable in regulatory submissions. Sustained MRD negativity — defined as MRD negativity confirmed at two consecutive assessments at least 12 months apart — is a more stringent and prognostically powerful endpoint than single-timepoint MRD negativity. FDA's January 2026 draft guidance proposed MRD negativity (single timepoint) and sustained MRD negativity as endpoints capable of supporting accelerated approval in transplant-eligible NDMM and relapsed/refractory settings, pending validation of the MRD–OS surrogate relationship. In clinical trials, MRD negativity rate is reported as a proportion with 95% CI, and MRD negativity as a time-to-event endpoint (time to MRD negativity, duration of MRD negativity) is an emerging analytical approach.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: MRD negativity, representing the deepest currently measurable haematological response, is theoretically associated with the lowest residual disease burden and thus the greatest potential for PRO benefit through disease control; however, prospective PRO data stratified by MRD status are sparse, and the MRD negativity–PRO correlation has not been formally validated. An AI agent should treat MRD negativity as a promising but unvalidated PRO predictor, flag the absence of prospective PRO–MRD analyses as a data gap, and note that MRD assessment burden (bone marrow sampling) may transiently worsen PRO scores at testing timepoints.

Short_Definition: The proportion of myeloma patients achieving PR or deeper (VGPR, CR, sCR) per IMWG Uniform Response Criteria.
Extended_Definition: In the myeloma-specific context, ORR is defined as the proportion of patients in the evaluable or ITT population achieving a confirmed best response of partial response (PR) or deeper — encompassing VGPR, CR, and sCR — per IMWG Uniform Response Criteria, assessed by a designated response evaluator using scheduled M-protein, sFLC, urine, and bone marrow assessments. This definition is narrower than some solid tumour ORR definitions (which may include minor responses) and excludes minimal response (MR, 25–49% M-protein reduction), stable disease, and MRD negativity as ORR components. ORR in myeloma requires confirmation of response at a consecutive assessment ≥4 weeks after the first documented response to exclude transient M-protein fluctuations; stringent confirmation requirements may differ between trial protocols and should be verified in the response assessment section of the SAP. FDA has accepted myeloma ORR as the basis for accelerated approval in relapsed/refractory settings when the response rate and durability are considered clinically meaningful given the unmet need; durability is typically characterised by DOR and supported by PFS data. The ORR composite in myeloma is often presented as a waterfall plot showing individual patient M-protein changes from baseline, providing a visual complement to the summary response statistics.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: In the myeloma-specific context, ORR encompasses a heterogeneous mix of response depths (PR through sCR) with substantially different PRO implications: PR patients may show marginal PRO improvement while sCR patients may experience near-complete symptom relief, meaning ORR as a composite obscures the PRO benefit distribution. An AI agent should always decompose myeloma ORR into response depth strata when analysing PRO correlations, and resist using ORR as a monolithic predictor of PRO outcomes without depth-stratified data.

Example_In_Context: In the ELOQUENT-2 trial, ORR per IMWG criteria was 79% in the elotuzumab arm versus 66% in the control arm (p<0.001); PRO analysis stratified by best response showed that patients achieving ≥VGPR in both arms reported significantly better EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status scores at month 6 than PR-only patients, confirming that the ORR composite masked important PRO heterogeneity across response depths.

Short_Definition: The proportion of patients achieving minimal response or deeper, including MR, PR, VGPR, CR, and sCR per IMWG criteria.
Extended_Definition: CBR extends ORR by including minimal response (MR) — defined as a 25–49% reduction in serum M-protein — as an additional response category, producing a broader composite of patients who derive some degree of tumour reduction from treatment beyond stable disease. CBR is particularly relevant in heavily pretreated relapsed/refractory myeloma populations where achieving PR or better may be less common, and where any degree of sustained tumour reduction — even MR — may be associated with symptom relief and extended TTNT. The clinical value of MR as a meaningful response is debated: some analyses suggest MR provides only modest and inconsistent PFS benefit compared with stable disease, while others demonstrate meaningful OS advantage in specific patient subgroups. CBR is not accepted by FDA as a primary endpoint for accelerated approval — ORR (≥PR) remains the standard — but is commonly reported as a secondary or supportive endpoint in single-arm trials and in compassionate use settings. In myeloma trials involving elderly, frail, or multi-refractory patients, CBR provides a more sensitive measure of clinical activity than ORR and better reflects the treatment benefit achievable in this population.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: CBR includes MR patients, whose degree of tumour reduction (25–49%) may or may not reach the threshold for patient-perceptible symptom relief — making CBR an even more heterogeneous predictor of PRO outcomes than ORR. Short_Definition: Time from baseline to a predefined worsening in patient-reported pain score, typically on the BPI-SF, meeting a threshold indicative of meaningful deterioration.

Short_Definition: A predefined rise in prostate-specific antigen level meeting PCWG criteria for biochemical disease progression in prostate cancer.

Short_Definition: A ≥50% decline in PSA from baseline, confirmed at a consecutive assessment ≥4 weeks later, used as a biochemical response indicator in prostate cancer.

Short_Definition: The proportion of patients achieving a predefined improvement in organ function affected by amyloid deposition, assessed per consensus criteria in AL amyloidosis.

Short_Definition: The frequency of treatment administration, defining the cycle length and consequently the timing of scheduled PRO assessments anchored to cycle days.
Extended_Definition: The treatment schedule defines the interval between repeated drug administrations, with Q28D (every 28 days, 4-week cycle) and Q21D (every 21 days, 3-week cycle) being the most common cycle lengths in haematological oncology; other schedules include Q7D (weekly), Q14D (biweekly), QD (daily oral), and Q42D (6-week cycles used for some monoclonal antibodies). The cycle length is operationally critical for PRO assessment design because PRO questionnaires are typically scheduled at Day 1 of each cycle, meaning Q21D regimens generate PRO assessments every 3 weeks and Q28D regimens every 4 weeks across the same calendar period — producing different longitudinal data densities and different exposure to within-cycle symptom fluctuations. In myeloma trials involving combination regimens with different cycle lengths across agents (e.g., daratumumab Q28D after initial Q7D loading), the transition in dosing frequency must be explicitly addressed in the PRO assessment schedule to avoid gaps or assessment timing ambiguity. The dosing schedule also determines the temporal resolution at which treatment-related toxicity dynamics — such as nadir cytopenias in chemotherapy regimens — are captured in PRO data, as within-cycle symptom variation may be missed if assessments occur only at cycle Day 1. Regulatory submissions must document the rationale for PRO assessment frequency relative to the dosing schedule and demonstrate that the schedule adequately captures clinically relevant symptom dynamics.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The treatment schedule determines the temporal resolution of longitudinal PRO data: Q21D cycles produce 17% more PRO timepoints per year than Q28D cycles, and within-cycle toxicity nadirs may be completely missed by Day 1–only assessments regardless of cycle length. An AI agent comparing PRO trajectories across trials must account for differences in assessment frequency driven by cycle schedule before attributing differences in observed PRO burden to treatment effects rather than measurement timing.

Short_Definition: A treatment duration rule specifying that patients continue receiving study treatment until the occurrence of disease progression per protocol-defined criteria.
Extended_Definition: Until progressive disease is a treatment duration specification in oncology trial protocols indicating that study treatment is administered continuously until the investigator documents disease progression meeting the protocol's prespecified response criteria — such as IMWG progression criteria in myeloma — or until another stopping criterion is met (unacceptable toxicity, patient withdrawal, death, or investigator decision). This open-ended treatment duration creates a variable exposure period across patients that must be explicitly addressed in the PRO assessment schedule: patients who progress early contribute only a few PRO assessments, while long-term responders contribute data across many cycles, producing an inherently unbalanced longitudinal dataset. For TTD and TTDD analyses, progression and treatment discontinuation due to progression are typically associated with censoring decisions or informative dropout depending on the estimand specification under ICH E9(R1). PRO assessments must be scheduled not only at on-treatment cycle days but also at the EOT visit (at time of progression or discontinuation) to capture the patient's PRO status at the endpoint event. In myeloma trials, "until PD" treatment duration means that some patients on effective regimens may remain on treatment and completing PRO assessments for years, while the majority progress within the median PFS timeframe.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Open-ended "until PD" treatment duration creates informative dropout by design: patients who progress — and thus stop treatment and PRO completion — typically have worse PRO trajectories than continuing patients, making missing data MNAR by assumption. An AI agent must flag "until PD" protocols as high missing-data-risk designs and verify that the SAP includes pre-specified MNAR sensitivity analyses for all longitudinal PRO endpoints.

Short_Definition: The final protocol-mandated clinical and PRO assessment conducted at or shortly after treatment discontinuation for any reason.
Extended_Definition: The end of treatment (EOT) visit is a scheduled protocol assessment conducted at the time of or immediately following a patient's last dose of study treatment, capturing the patient's clinical status and PRO scores at the moment of treatment cessation regardless of the reason for discontinuation. EOT visits are critical for PRO analysis because they provide the last on-treatment observation for patients who discontinue due to progression, toxicity, or withdrawal, and anchor the transition from on-treatment to post-treatment follow-up PRO assessment schedules. The EOT PRO assessment is particularly important for TTD and TTDD analyses, as it may constitute the defining deterioration event for patients who show PRO worsening coinciding with treatment cessation, and its timing and completion rate directly affect the validity of censoring in time-to-event PRO analyses. EOT visits must be distinguished from final-assessment visits in long-term follow-up: patients who complete planned treatment (e.g., fixed-duration regimens) have EOT visits at treatment completion in a non-distressed state, while patients discontinuing for progression or toxicity have EOT visits coinciding with clinical deterioration, creating a heterogeneous PRO dataset at this timepoint. Protocol windows for EOT PRO completion (typically within 7–14 days of last dose) must be defined and enforced to ensure temporal alignment of EOT PRO scores with the clinical discontinuation event.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: EOT PRO assessments capture symptom status at the clinically critical transition point between on-treatment and post-treatment observation, making them essential for characterising the PRO impact of treatment discontinuation and for correctly attributing censoring in TTD analyses. An AI agent should flag low EOT PRO completion rates as a major missing data risk, particularly for patients discontinuing due to progression or toxicity, whose EOT PRO scores are the most clinically informative and the most likely to be MNAR.

Short_Definition: A scheduled post-treatment assessment occurring after the EOT visit, used to monitor disease status, survival, and post-treatment PRO trajectory.
Extended_Definition: Follow-up visits are protocol-mandated assessments conducted at regular intervals after a patient completes or discontinues study treatment, serving to monitor disease status, document progression events, collect survival data, and — in PRO-inclusive designs — capture post-treatment patient-reported outcomes. Follow-up visits are particularly important in myeloma trials with "until PD" treatment design, where patients who progress and discontinue treatment continue to be followed for OS, subsequent therapy data (TTNT), and sometimes post-treatment PRO assessments. Post-treatment PRO data collected during follow-up visits provide critical evidence for long-term HRQoL trajectory, capturing the patient experience after treatment cessation including recovery from toxicity, disease progression symptom burden, and the impact of subsequent salvage therapy initiation. The frequency of follow-up PRO assessments is typically reduced relative to on-treatment schedules (e.g., every 12 weeks post-EOT vs. every cycle on-treatment) to balance data richness against patient burden in a period when many patients are receiving subsequent therapies that complicate PRO attribution. Regulatory submissions should specify whether post-treatment PRO data are used in the primary analysis, as sensitivity analyses, or as exploratory endpoints, and should address the interpretation challenge posed by subsequent therapies confounding post-EOT PRO scores.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Post-treatment follow-up PRO assessments capture the long-term patient experience beyond treatment — including both recovery from treatment-related toxicity and disease progression burden — but are confounded by subsequent therapies, making interpretation challenging without stratification by post-EOT treatment status. An AI agent should distinguish on-treatment PRO assessments from follow-up PRO assessments and flag the onset of subsequent therapy as a confounding intercurrent event in any post-EOT PRO analysis.

Short_Definition: The prespecified allowable time range around a scheduled assessment date within which a PRO or clinical measurement is considered protocol-compliant.
Extended_Definition: A window period (or assessment window) defines the acceptable time interval — typically expressed as ±X days around the target assessment date — within which a PRO questionnaire completion or clinical measurement is considered to have occurred "on schedule" for the purposes of data analysis and compliance reporting. For example, a Cycle 3 Day 1 PRO with a ±3-day window means that questionnaires completed between Day −2 and Day +4 relative to the target date are treated as on-time cycle 3 assessments. Window periods must be prespecified in the protocol and SAP, and the chosen width reflects a balance between operational feasibility (allowing for scheduling flexibility and patient convenience) and scientific precision (ensuring that assessments are temporally aligned across patients for time-point-specific analyses). If a patient completes a PRO assessment outside the specified window, the observation may be excluded from that visit's analysis, treated as the nearest scheduled visit, or handled per specific out-of-window rules defined in the SAP. Narrow windows reduce timing variability but increase missing data rates; wide windows allow more observations to be counted but introduce temporal heterogeneity that can bias time-point analyses. In regulatory submissions, the window period definitions and their impact on the proportion of assessments classified as in-window vs. out-of-window must be reported transparently.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Window period definitions directly determine how many PRO assessments are classified as protocol-compliant and included in time-point-specific analyses; overly narrow windows increase apparent missing data rates and can artificially reduce completion rates below regulatory thresholds. An AI agent must extract and apply window period rules from the SAP when classifying PRO observations as on-time, out-of-window, or missing, and flag any post-hoc changes to window period definitions as a potential source of analysis bias.

Example_In_Context: The PRO assessment window was defined as ±3 days for on-treatment cycle Day 1 visits and ±7 days for follow-up visits; out-of-window assessments (4.2% of all observations) were excluded from time-point-specific MMRM analyses but included in the TTD analysis using their actual completion date, as pre-specified in the SAP.

Short_Definition: The timeframe over which patients are asked to retrospectively report their symptoms or functioning when completing a PRO instrument.
Extended_Definition: The recall period is the time interval specified in the instructions of a PRO instrument over which respondents are asked to reflect when answering items — for example "over the past 7 days," "over the past 24 hours," or "right now" (momentary assessment). Recall period is a fundamental design attribute of PRO instruments that must match the temporal dynamics of the concept being measured: rapidly fluctuating acute symptoms (e.g., nausea, acute pain) require short recall periods (24-hour or momentary) to minimise recall bias, while stable constructs (e.g., global functioning, role function) may be reliably captured with 7-day recall. The EORTC QLQ-C30 uses a 1-week recall period for most items, the BPI-SF uses 24-hour recall for worst and least pain and "right now" for current pain intensity, and FACIT instruments typically use 7-day recall; modifying the recall period of a validated instrument even slightly invalidates existing psychometric evidence and requires full re-validation. Mismatches between the recall period and the assessment schedule create systematic data gaps: a 7-day recall instrument completed every 28 days captures only the final week of each cycle, leaving three weeks of the patient's symptom experience unobserved per cycle.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Recall period mismatches with assessment frequency are a major but frequently underappreciated source of systematic measurement error in PRO trials; an AI agent must verify that the recall period of each PROM is compatible with the trial's assessment schedule and flag protocols where assessments are spaced more widely than the instrument's recall window, as these produce structurally incomplete symptom data that cannot be recovered analytically.

Short_Definition: The prespecified period around each scheduled PRO assessment date within which completion is counted as protocol-compliant and included in the primary analysis.
Extended_Definition: The PRO assessment compliance window is the operationally defined time interval — distinct from the broader clinical visit window period (Term 93) — within which a patient must complete a PRO questionnaire for that assessment to be counted as protocol-compliant and included in visit-specific analyses such as MMRM time-point estimates and per-visit completion rate calculations. For example, a compliance window of −1 to +3 days around cycle Day 1 means that questionnaires completed between the day before and three days after the target date are counted as on-schedule; responses outside this window may be excluded from time-point analyses or reassigned to the nearest scheduled visit per SAP rules. The compliance window interacts critically with the instrument's recall period (Term 94): if the compliance window is wide relative to the recall period, questionnaires completed at different points within the window may be referencing partially non-overlapping symptom experiences, introducing heterogeneity at the nominally same assessment timepoint. Compliance window definitions must be prespecified in the SAP, applied consistently across all sites and patients, and reported transparently in publications and regulatory submissions along with the proportion of assessments falling within versus outside the window. Electronic PRO (ePRO) platforms with time-stamped completion data enable precise compliance window adjudication and should be preferred over paper PRO for regulatory submissions.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The PRO compliance window directly determines what proportion of collected assessments are analysable in the primary MMRM and time-point-specific analyses; a poorly chosen or post-hoc modified compliance window can artificially inflate or deflate per-visit completion rates and alter the observed treatment comparison. An AI agent must extract the compliance window specification from the SAP before calculating or interpreting per-visit PRO completion rates, and flag any post-protocol changes to window definitions as a potential source of analysis bias.

Short_Definition: Proportion of patients with measurable intracranial lesions achieving confirmed complete or partial response by CNS imaging criteria.
Extended_Definition: OIRR is defined as the proportion of patients with measurable intracranial disease — typically ≥1 brain lesion ≥10 mm in longest diameter on gadolinium-enhanced MRI — who achieve confirmed CR or PR per CNS-specific response criteria, most commonly RANO-BM (Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology - Brain Metastases) criteria, with confirmation at a second scan ≥4 weeks after initial response. It is used as a primary or co-primary endpoint in trials specifically designed to demonstrate intracranial activity in indications with high CNS metastasis rates, such as HER2+ breast cancer, EGFR-mutant NSCLC, and melanoma with brain involvement; in multiple myeloma, it applies to the rare setting of CNS myeloma or cerebral plasmacytoma, where no universally standardised CNS MM-specific response criteria exist. OIRR is distinct from systemic ORR and may diverge substantially when an agent has limited blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration that produces extracranial control without meaningful intracranial activity. Regulatory acceptance of OIRR as a primary endpoint typically requires prospective enrolment of patients with active, measurable intracranial disease rather than post-hoc subgroup analysis in a broader trial. In CNS myeloma, MRI-based assessment per modified RANO or investigator-defined criteria is required, and OIRR data are generally treated as exploratory given the rarity of evaluable CNS disease in pivotal myeloma trials.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: CNS disease produces a distinct, severe symptom profile — headache, cognitive impairment, seizures, motor deficits, and neuropathic pain — that standard myeloma PRO instruments (EORTC QLQ-C30, FACT-MM) are not validated to capture; intracranial response should therefore be cross-referenced with CNS-specific PRO instruments such as FACT-Brain or MDASI-Brain Tumor to assess patient-perceived neurological benefit. An AI agent must flag the absence of validated CNS myeloma PRO instruments as a data gap when OIRR is an endpoint and recommend supplementary cognitive and neurological symptom assessment tools to capture the full PRO impact of intracranial disease activity.

Example_In_Context: OIRR was 73.9% (95% CI 51.6–89.8) in 46 patients with active brain metastases receiving the CNS-penetrant agent; concurrent FACT-Brain subscale scores improved by a mean of 7.2 points from baseline in intracranial responders versus −0.4 points in non-responders, confirming patient-perceived neurological benefit concordant with the imaging-defined intracranial response.

Short_Definition: Proportion of patients with intracranial disease achieving CR, PR, or stable disease by CNS imaging criteria.
Extended_Definition: IDCR is a composite endpoint defined as the proportion of patients with measurable or evaluable intracranial disease achieving a best intracranial response of CR, PR, or stable disease (SD) of at least a minimum duration — typically ≥6–8 weeks — per CNS-specific response criteria such as RANO-BM, extending OIRR by including patients who achieve disease stabilisation without meeting the threshold for objective intracranial response. IDCR is particularly relevant in CNS disease settings where BBB-limiting drug penetration results in low OIRR even when systemic disease is well-controlled, and where intracranial stabilisation — preventing further CNS lesion growth — is itself a clinically meaningful benefit for symptomatic patients. Stable intracranial disease and intracranial CR/PR have distinct PRO implications: SD patients experience neither neurological improvement nor worsening, while CR/PR patients are expected to show meaningful PRO improvement in cognitive and neurological domains, making IDCR a heterogeneous PRO predictor without response-depth stratification. IDCR differs from ICBR (Term 99) in the minimum SD duration applied: IDCR requires only a minimum confirmation interval (≥6–8 weeks), while ICBR typically requires ≥6 months of maintained SD, producing a more stringent clinical benefit determination. In CNS myeloma, IDCR is used as a descriptive measure of intracranial treatment activity given the absence of standardised CNS MM response criteria.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Like its systemic analogue (DCR, Term 61), IDCR encompasses response-depth heterogeneous patients with divergent PRO trajectories: intracranial CR/PR patients typically report meaningful neurological symptom improvement on CNS-specific PRO instruments, while SD patients show symptom stabilisation. An AI agent should decompose IDCR by response depth and cross-reference with CNS PRO instrument scores to avoid overinterpreting IDCR as uniform evidence of patient-perceived intracranial benefit.

Example_In_Context: IDCR was 91.3% in the CNS-penetrant experimental arm versus 65.2% in the standard arm (p=0.004); PRO analyses of the FACT-Brain cognitive subscale showed clinically meaningful improvement (≥7-point increase) only in intracranial CR/PR patients (63% responder rate) and not in intracranial SD patients (11% responder rate), confirming the response-depth dependency of patient-perceived CNS benefit within the IDCR composite.

Short_Definition: Time from first confirmed intracranial response to intracranial progression or death in patients achieving an intracranial response.
Extended_Definition: DOIR is a time-to-event endpoint calculated from the date of first confirmed intracranial response (CR or PR per applicable CNS criteria) to the date of first documented intracranial progression or death from any cause, calculated only in patients who achieved a confirmed intracranial response, making it a response-conditioned, selection-biased estimate analogous to systemic DOR (Term 60). DOIR characterises the durability of intracranial tumour control and is an essential complement to OIRR: a high OIRR with short DOIR provides substantially less sustained patient benefit than a moderate OIRR with prolonged responses, as brief intracranial responses may produce only transient symptomatic improvement followed by rapid neurological deterioration. DOIR is analysed using Kaplan-Meier estimation, with median DOIR and landmark response duration rates (e.g., proportion maintaining intracranial response at 6 and 12 months) as key summary statistics; patients with ongoing intracranial response at last assessment are censored at last evaluable brain imaging date. In comparative randomised trials, DOIR should be interpreted alongside arm-level differences in OIRR, as longer DOIR in one arm may reflect selection of a more favourable-prognosis responding subgroup rather than a genuine pharmacological durability advantage. In the rare CNS myeloma context, DOIR is not standardised and is typically reported descriptively with wide confidence intervals due to small patient numbers.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: DOIR determines whether intracranial responses translate into sustained PRO benefit in cognitive and neurological domains; short DOIR followed by rapid intracranial relapse is expected to produce a transient PRO improvement arc detectable in CNS-specific instruments if assessment frequency is sufficient to capture the rise and fall. An AI agent should cross-reference median DOIR estimates with the temporal trajectory of CNS PRO instrument scores to assess whether the duration of intracranial tumour control is adequate to produce durable patient-perceived neurological benefit.

Short_Definition: Proportion of patients achieving intracranial CR, PR, or durable stable disease meeting a minimum predefined duration criterion.
Extended_Definition: Intracranial clinical benefit rate is a composite endpoint representing the proportion of patients with evaluable intracranial disease achieving a best intracranial response of CR, PR, or stable disease maintained for at least a predefined minimum duration — most commonly ≥6 months per RANO-BM or protocol-defined criteria — distinguishing it from IDCR, which applies a shorter minimum SD confirmation interval of only ≥6–8 weeks. The minimum SD duration requirement ensures that brief transient stabilisations — which may reflect natural disease plateau rather than pharmacological activity — are excluded, producing a more conservative and clinically defensible measure of intracranial benefit than IDCR. ICBR is most relevant in CNS disease settings where prolonged intracranial stabilisation is itself a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly for patients with previously treated brain metastases or for therapies with primarily cytostatic CNS mechanisms. The PRO implications of the durable SD component are distinct from those of CR/PR: patients with ≥6-month intracranial SD experience preservation rather than improvement in CNS symptom burden, and their PRO profiles are expected to show stability rather than meaningful score gains on CNS-specific instruments. ICBR is not standardised in myeloma-specific regulatory guidance and is primarily encountered in solid tumour CNS metastasis trial literature.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: The durable SD component of ICBR represents neurological symptom preservation rather than improvement — a distinct and PRO-measurable clinical state separable from both responding patients (PRO improvement) and progressing patients (PRO deterioration) in serial CNS PRO assessments. An AI agent should decompose ICBR by response depth and model the expected PRO trajectory profile for each subgroup — improvement for CR/PR, preservation for durable SD — to generate response-conditional PRO benefit characterisations rather than applying a uniform ICBR-level PRO inference.

Short_Definition: The quantitative characterisation of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion and their relationship to drug exposure over time.
Extended_Definition: Pharmacokinetics encompasses the mathematical description of how a drug moves through the body over time, characterised by parameters including maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), area under the concentration-time curve (AUC), time to maximum concentration (Tmax), half-life (t½), clearance (CL), and volume of distribution (Vd). In the context of PRO-inclusive clinical trials, PK parameters are relevant because drug exposure level is a key determinant of both therapeutic efficacy — and therefore haematological response depth and associated PRO improvement — and toxicity burden — and therefore treatment-related symptom burden captured by PRO instruments. PK–PRO exposure-response analyses explore whether higher drug exposure correlates with greater PRO benefit (supporting dose intensity) or with greater treatment-related PRO burden (informing tolerability-based dose modifications). Population PK modelling enables identification of patient subgroups with altered drug exposure — due to renal impairment, hepatic dysfunction, age, or drug interactions — whose PRO profiles may differ systematically from the overall trial population. FDA's Project Optimus initiative explicitly calls for PK–PRO exposure-response data to inform dose optimisation in oncology, making PK–PRO integration a growing regulatory priority.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: PK–PRO exposure-response analyses are increasingly expected by FDA under Project Optimus to demonstrate that the selected dose optimises the benefit–PRO burden trade-off rather than simply maximising tumour response; an AI agent should flag the presence or absence of PK–PRO analyses in oncology submissions as a regulatory completeness indicator and cross-reference dose modification rates with concurrent PRO trajectory changes to assess real-world tolerability.

Example_In_Context: Population PK modelling demonstrated that patients in the highest AUC quartile had a 2.3-fold higher rate of grade ≥3 peripheral neuropathy compared with the lowest quartile; concurrent BPI-SF pain interference scores were 4.1 points higher in the highest versus lowest exposure quartile at cycle 3, supporting a PK–PRO exposure-toxicity relationship that informed the protocol amendment reducing the starting dose in subsequent cohorts.

Short_Definition: The proportion of patients with measurable bone lesions achieving a predefined improvement in bone disease by imaging criteria.
Extended_Definition: Bone tumour response rate is defined as the proportion of patients with measurable skeletal lesions achieving a predefined improvement — typically reduction in size, number, or metabolic activity of lytic or sclerotic bone lesions — assessed by CT, MRI, whole-body low-dose CT (WBLDCT), or PET-CT per protocol-specified skeletal imaging criteria. In multiple myeloma, WBLDCT has become the standard-of-care imaging modality for bone disease assessment, with PET-CT increasingly used for metabolic response evaluation and MRI reserved for axial disease and cord compression; RECIST criteria are not applicable to myeloma bone disease given the predominantly lytic, non-measurable nature of most lesions. Bone imaging response in myeloma is typically assessed qualitatively (new lesion appearance or documented healing of known lesions) rather than using RECIST-style unidimensional measurements, and it is not currently incorporated into IMWG Uniform Response Criteria as a standalone response component. Bone imaging response is closely linked to SRE risk reduction and to patient-reported bone pain improvement: lesions that show healing on imaging are expected to be associated with reduced pain and improved physical functioning in PRO assessments, though the correlation is imperfect due to the time lag between haematological response, bone remodelling, and structural healing. BTRR is most commonly encountered as an exploratory or secondary endpoint in bone-targeting agent trials (bisphosphonates, denosumab, anti-sclerostin antibodies) and in trials evaluating novel osteoclast/osteoblast-targeting therapies in myeloma.
Why_It_Matters_For_PRO: Bone tumour imaging response should be cross-referenced with concurrent BPI-SF worst pain and pain interference scores and EORTC QLQ-C30 physical functioning data to validate whether imaging-defined bone healing translates into patient-perceived pain relief and functional improvement; discordance between structural bone response and PRO pain trajectories is a clinically important signal indicating ongoing neuropathic or structural pain independent of active osteolysis. An AI agent should model bone tumour response as a mechanistic mediator — rather than a direct proxy — of PRO pain improvement, and require concurrent PRO data before inferring patient-perceived benefit from imaging-based bone disease response.

Example_In_Context: Bone imaging response — defined as healing or no new lytic lesions on WBLDCT at cycle 6 — was achieved in 71% of patients in the zoledronic acid arm; patients with bone imaging response reported a mean BPI-SF worst pain score of 2.8 at cycle 6 compared with 4.9 in non-responders, supporting the expected directional concordance between structural bone response and patient-perceived pain relief, though the between-group BPI-SF difference of 2.1 points fell below the pre-specified 2-point MID for a group-level pain claim.
